title: An Exposition of the Old Testament
author: John Gill
allowedUseNotes: Public-domain 18th-century commentary (published 1748-1763, long pre-1928). May be cited, quoted in short excerpt, or paraphrased freely with attribution; no full-chapter reproduction needed per this project's own tighter internal policy regardless.
summary: Verse-by-verse exposition of the whole Bible by the English Baptist minister and Hebraist John Gill, one of the more philologically detailed 18th-century Protestant commentaries, drawing heavily on rabbinic sources (Targum, Kimchi/Radak, Solomon ben Melech's Mikhlal Yofi, and others). On 1 Samuel 31:12, Gill reports that the Aramaic Targum renders the verse as the men of Jabesh 'burning over' the bodies rather than burning the bodies themselves, comparing it to the ceremonial burning of spices or of a deceased king's bedding/household goods attested for later Judahite royal funerals (e.g. 2 Chronicles 16:14) — an interpretive tradition Gill attributes to the Targum and reports as also discussed by Kimchi and Ben Melech, though Gill notes those two commentators ultimately prefer the plain reading that the flesh itself was burned (with the bones then buried separately). Gill's own reasoning for why the flesh was burned in this case includes the possibility that the bodies were already putrid from days of exposure on Beth-shan's wall, and/or that burning was meant to keep the remains out of Philistine hands if they returned. On 2 Samuel 1:6, Gill flags specific discrepancies between the Amalekite messenger's account and 1 Samuel 31's own narration and judges the messenger's story unreliable on its own internal evidence: the messenger says Saul was 'leaning on his spear' when he came upon him, which Gill notes 'seems not true, for he fell upon his sword for that purpose' per 1 Samuel 31:4; and the messenger's claim that 'the chariots and the horsemen followed hard after him' does not match 1 Samuel 31:3's own account, where it is archers who overtake Saul. Gill reads the crown and armlet the messenger produces (2 Samuel 1:10) as probably genuine (taken as a battlefield looter, confirming that Saul was in fact dead), while treating his narrated claim to have personally struck the death-blow, along with these specific circumstantial details, as invented to secure standing and a reward from David.
